questions.text: A hospital discovers that a patient received a blood transfusion intended for a different patient and survived without permanent harm only because a nurse noticed the discrepancy mid-transfusion and stopped it. How should this event be classified?

options.a: Medical Error — because a planned action failed
options.b: Near Miss — because the system failed but no harm reached the patient
options.c: Adverse Event — because the patient received wrong blood products
options.d: Sentinel Event — because wrong blood transfusion always triggers mandatory RCA

questions.explanation: A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but did not — either by chance or timely intervention. The system failed (wrong blood was prepared and nearly administered), but the timely intervention prevented harm from reaching the patient. Root causes still exist and must be investigated with full rigor.

questions.text: A hospital quality team wants to supplement its voluntary incident reporting system to detect harm that staff may not be reporting. Which tool is specifically designed to identify unreported adverse events through retrospective chart review?
questions.explanation: The GTT is a retrospective chart review methodology developed by IHI that uses predefined clinical triggers (e.g., naloxone use, return to operating room) to identify adverse events that may not be captured through voluntary reporting. It detects significantly more harm than traditional reporting alone.

questions.text: A hospital's safety committee reviews a case in which a surgeon left a sponge inside a patient after abdominal surgery. The committee determines this qualifies as a Serious Reportable Event. Which of the following consequences is most directly associated with this classification?

options.a: Mandatory peer review and possible medical staff suspension
options.b: CMS may deny reimbursement for costs related to the event
options.c: The hospital must self-report to TJC within 24 hours
options.d: The event is classified as ameliorable rather than preventable

questions.explanation: NQF Serious Reportable Events (Never Events) represent major system failures that should never occur in a properly functioning healthcare system. CMS enforces a non-payment policy for costs associated with Never Events, and the NQF defines the categories including this classic surgical example.

questions.text: A quality professional is selecting the best tool to measure whether staff feel psychologically safe reporting errors and whether leadership actively supports safety. Which tool is most appropriate?

options.b: AHRQ Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture (HSOPS)

questions.explanation: AHRQ HSOPS is a validated, standardized survey tool that measures staff perceptions of safety culture across domains including teamwork, communication, reporting, staffing, and leadership support. It measures the CONDITIONS that cause harm — not harm itself — making it the appropriate tool for assessing psychological safety and leadership engagement.

questions.text: A nurse reports a medication error through the hospital's internal reporting system. The hospital is a member of a Patient Safety Organization (PSO). Under PSQIA, which protection applies to the nurse's report?

options.a: The report is protected from regulatory inspection by TJC
options.b: The report constitutes Patient Safety Work Product and is legally protected from use in litigation
options.c: The nurse cannot be disciplined for the error because the report was filed with the PSO
options.d: The report is automatically shared with CMS for public reporting purposes

questions.explanation: Under the Patient Safety and Quality Improvement Act (PSQIA), information submitted to a PSO becomes Patient Safety Work Product (PSWP) and is legally protected from discovery in litigation. This protection exists specifically to encourage honest, candid reporting without fear of legal exposure.
